headline: MSPB Narrows Federal Employee Appeal Jurisdiction
dek: Starting Sept. 2, most new probationary-termination, suitability and reduction-in-force appeals move out of the Merit Systems Protection Board, while earlier matters and Foreign Service RIF cases remain.

lead.creator: Another Believer
lead.rightsBasis: The photographer licensed the documentary federal-office photograph CC BY-SA 3.0 on Wikimedia Commons.
lead.caption: The Office of Personnel Management building in Washington in 2012. OPM rules prompted the Merit Systems Protection Board to revise its list of appealable actions.
lead.alt: Stone federal office building with an Office of Personnel Management sign in Washington.

charts.caption: The Sept. 2 framework removes MSPB regulatory jurisdiction for most new probationary-termination, suitability and general RIF appeals.
charts.alt: Graphic lists probationary termination, suitability and reduction-in-force appeals moving from MSPB jurisdiction.

charts.caption: Pending and pre-effective-date matters remain with MSPB, as does its statutory jurisdiction over Foreign Service RIF appeals.
charts.alt: Graphic lists pending cases, earlier agency actions and Foreign Service RIF appeals as retained MSPB matters.

paragraphs: The Merit Systems Protection Board has revised its jurisdiction list to remove regulatory references for most new probationary-termination, suitability and reduction-in-force appeals beginning Sept. 2.

The final rule follows Office of Personnel Management rules that rescinded the regulatory bases for those MSPB appeals and directed the affected appeal paths to OPM. The MSPB says its own revision reflects those decisions rather than independently creating the shift.

Timing determines the forum. The board will continue adjudicating probationary-termination and suitability appeals already pending on Sept. 2, along with qualifying matters tied to agency actions taken before the OPM rules become effective.

For reductions in force, MSPB says an appeal may remain in its process when the agency issued the employee's specific RIF notice before Sept. 2. A later filing date alone does not necessarily move an earlier action out of MSPB.
The rule also keeps the board's separate statutory jurisdiction over RIF appeals by career or career-candidate Foreign Service appointees under 22 U.S.C. 4010a.

Suitability actions named in the record include cancellation of eligibility, removal, cancellation of reinstatement eligibility and debarment. The rule does not say every other kind of personnel dispute is barred from MSPB review.

MSPB issued the amendment without prior notice and comment, saying it lacked discretion because OPM had rescinded the underlying regulatory jurisdiction. The board classified the action as significant but below the $100 million annual-effects threshold.

Federal workers facing an individual deadline should use the operative agency notice and current rules for their case. This report describes the jurisdiction change and is not individualized legal advice.
facts: The final rule takes effect Sept. 2, 2026.
Most new probationary-termination, suitability and general RIF appeals lose their cited MSPB regulatory basis.
Pending and qualifying pre-effective-date matters can continue at MSPB.
Foreign Service RIF jurisdiction remains under statute.
uncertainty: The correct forum for a particular case can depend on the agency-action date and type of appointment.
Later litigation or rulemaking could alter the described framework.
seoTitle: MSPB federal employee appeal jurisdiction changes Sept. 2
seoDescription: MSPB's 2026 rule moves most new probationary, suitability and RIF appeals out of its regulatory jurisdiction while preserving earlier matters and Foreign Service cases.

headline: U.S. Restricts Imports of Protected Nepalese Cultural Objects
dek: The five-year agreement covers designated archaeological material dating to about 32,000 B.C.E. and specified religious, ceremonial and manuscript material through 1950.

sources.title: Imposition of Import Restrictions on Categories of Archaeological and Ethnological Material of Nepal

lead.creator: Nirmal Dulal
lead.rightsBasis: The photographer licensed the documentary architectural photograph CC BY-SA 4.0 on Wikimedia Commons.
lead.caption: Swayambhunath's historic religious architecture in Nepal. The U.S. import rule covers designated categories of Nepalese archaeological and ethnological material, not the site itself.
lead.alt: Historic white and gold religious structures at Swayambhunath under a blue sky.

charts.caption: The designated list spans archaeological material from about 32,000 B.C.E. through 1770 and specified ethnological material from the 13th century through 1950.
charts.alt: Graphic shows date ranges for archaeological and ethnological material covered by the Nepal import rule.

charts.caption: The restrictions began Aug. 12, 2026, and are scheduled through Jan. 8, 2031, unless extended under the agreement.
charts.alt: Graphic shows the Nepal cultural-property import restriction running to January 8, 2031.

paragraphs: The United States has begun restricting imports of designated archaeological and ethnological material from Nepal under a bilateral cultural-property agreement.

The Customs and Border Protection final rule took effect Aug. 12. It adds Nepal to the federal list of countries covered by cultural-property import restrictions and publishes a detailed designated list.

Archaeological categories range from approximately 32,000 B.C.E. through 1770 C.E. The ethnological categories cover specified religious architectural elements, religious and ceremonial objects, and manuscripts from roughly the 13th century through 1950.

The list is representative rather than an inventory of every protected object. It includes categories across stone, metal, ceramic, wood, textiles, paintings, manuscripts and other materials, with the applicable description and date range controlling.

A covered object may enter the United States only when the conditions in 19 U.S.C. 2606 and the implementing customs rules are met. The restriction is therefore not a ban on all Nepalese art, crafts or lawful cultural exchange.

The bilateral agreement was signed Jan. 8, 2026. U.S. officials had determined that Nepal's cultural patrimony was at risk of pillage, that Nepal had taken protective measures and that import restrictions would provide a substantial deterrent benefit.
The restrictions are scheduled to expire Jan. 8, 2031. They may be extended in periods of no more than five years if the statutory findings still apply and there is no cause for suspension.

Collectors, museums and importers need object-specific provenance and export documentation. This article summarizes the federal rule and does not decide whether any particular object is eligible for entry.
facts: The rule took effect Aug. 12, 2026.
Archaeological categories date from about 32,000 B.C.E. through 1770 C.E.
Specified ethnological categories date from the 13th century through 1950.
The current restriction period runs through Jan. 8, 2031 unless extended.
uncertainty: Eligibility depends on an object's category, age, origin and documentation.
The agreement may be extended after the initial period if statutory conditions remain.
seoTitle: Nepal cultural-property import restrictions take effect in U.S.
seoDescription: New U.S. restrictions cover designated Nepalese archaeological and ethnological objects through Jan. 8, 2031, with lawful entry still possible under documentation rules.

headline: FAA Proposes Faster Boeing 787 Corrosion Inspections
dek: The proposal covers 116 U.S.-registered 787s after more severe corrosion reports and concerns that optional sealants may not allow enough installation time.

sources.title: Airworthiness Directives; The Boeing Company Airplanes

lead.creator: New York-air
lead.rightsBasis: The photographer licensed the documentary aircraft photograph CC BY-SA 4.0 on Wikimedia Commons.
lead.caption: A Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner in flight-test markings. The FAA proposal covers specified 787-8, 787-9 and 787-10 aircraft and is not a finding about this individual airplane.
lead.alt: Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner flying against a pale sky.

charts.caption: The FAA estimates the proposal would affect 116 U.S.-registered 787s and calls for work around 16 vertical-fin tension-bolt locations.
charts.alt: Graphic shows 116 U.S. aircraft and 16 vertical-fin bolt locations in the FAA proposal.

charts.caption: FAA estimates inspection, sealant work and bolt or nut installation at up to $38,260 per affected airplane, with total U.S.-operator cost up to $4.44 million for that action.
charts.alt: Graphic shows FAA cost estimates of 38,260 dollars per airplane and up to 4.44 million dollars across U.S. operators.

paragraphs: The Federal Aviation Administration is proposing shorter compliance times and additional records checks for Boeing 787 vertical-fin corrosion inspections.
The proposal would replace portions of a 2022 airworthiness directive for specified 787-8, 787-9 and 787-10 airplanes. Comments are due Sept. 28; the requirements are not yet a new final mandate.

FAA says later inspection reports found corrosion that was sometimes more severe than expected. It also determined that optional sealant types allowed by the existing directive may not provide enough working time to complete all bolt installations without damaging the seal.

The affected area includes 16 vertical-fin tension-bolt holes in the aluminum crown frame, composite deck and root fittings. Depending on aircraft history and configuration, work can include records review, detailed inspections, sealant and finish application, bolt and barrel-nut replacement, repairs and maintenance-program revisions.

FAA estimates that 116 U.S.-registered airplanes would be affected. For the inspection, sealant application and bolt or nut installation action, it estimates six labor hours plus $37,750 in parts, or $38,260 per airplane.

Applied across the U.S. fleet, that action could cost up to $4,438,160, according to the proposal. Separate records reviews are estimated at $85 per airplane, while FAA estimates an average 90 hours, or $7,650, per operator for a maintenance-program revision.
Those figures are regulatory estimates, not invoices for every operator. Actual work depends on prior maintenance, configuration, findings and any approved alternative method of compliance.

The unsafe condition described by FAA is undetected corrosion that could reduce structural integrity of the vertical fin and lead to loss of control. The agency will review comments before deciding whether to adopt, change or withdraw the proposal.
facts: Comments are due Sept. 28, 2026.
FAA estimates 116 U.S.-registered 787s would be affected.
The inspection area includes 16 vertical-fin tension-bolt locations.
FAA estimates up to $4,438,160 for the principal action across U.S. operators.
uncertainty: This is a proposed airworthiness directive, not a final rule.
Actual compliance work and cost would vary by aircraft condition, maintenance history and final requirements.
seoTitle: FAA proposes faster Boeing 787 vertical-fin corrosion work
seoDescription: FAA's 2026 Boeing 787 proposal targets vertical-fin bolt-hole corrosion, 116 U.S. aircraft and revised sealant procedures, with comments due Sept. 28.

headline: Chicago Belt Railway Seeks Approval for PTC Maintenance
dek: FRA is taking comments through Sept. 1 on four planned network-work windows; the railroad says it will not disable I-ETMS but brief communication losses could occur.

sources.title: Belt Railway Company of Chicago's Request To Amend Its Positive Train Control Safety Plan

lead.creator: Ken Lund
lead.rightsBasis: The photographer licensed the documentary rail-yard photograph CC BY-SA 2.0 on Wikimedia Commons.
lead.caption: The Belt Railway of Chicago's Clearing Yard in an archival photograph. The railroad has asked FRA to approve a safety-plan amendment for 2026 network maintenance.
lead.alt: Multiple freight-train tracks and railcars spread across the Belt Railway clearing yard in Chicago.

charts.caption: Belt Railway submitted the amendment Aug. 6; public comments are due Sept. 1; FRA can approve, condition or deny the request.
charts.alt: Graphic shows August 6 submission, September 1 comment date and FRA decision options.

charts.caption: The request covers four planned September and October network-maintenance windows and the possibility of brief, unplanned I-ETMS communication losses.
charts.alt: Graphic describes four planned maintenance windows and possible brief communication losses.

paragraphs: The Belt Railway Company of Chicago has asked federal regulators to approve a positive train control safety-plan amendment for network maintenance scheduled during four windows in September and October.
The Federal Railroad Administration is accepting comments through Sept. 1. Publication of the notice opens review; it does not mean FRA has approved the request.

Belt Railway submitted the amendment Aug. 6 for work on its operational-technology network. Because the request involves a material modification to an FRA-certified system, federal rules require public notice and an opportunity to comment.
The railroad says it does not plan to disable its Interoperable Electronic Train Management System, known as I-ETMS, and will take measures to avoid outages.

It also tells FRA that transient network behavior or unforeseen maintenance effects could cause brief communication losses between the system's back-office and onboard components. The request seeks approval for temporary outages that might occur during the planned windows.

Positive train control is designed to help prevent specified train-to-train collisions, overspeed derailments and other covered events. This filing concerns the certified system's maintenance plan, not a report that such an event occurred.

FRA can approve the amendment, approve it with conditions or deny it. The agency says it will consider timely comments and may consider later submissions when practicable without delaying valuable or necessary system modifications.

The public notice identifies the four-window request but does not itself establish the duration or operational effect of any outage. Final conditions, if any, will depend on FRA's review of the docket.
facts: Belt Railway submitted the amendment Aug. 6, 2026.
Comments are due Sept. 1, 2026.
The request covers four planned maintenance windows in September and October.
FRA retains authority to approve, condition or deny the request.
uncertainty: FRA has not yet decided the amendment.
The railroad says outages are possible but unplanned, so their occurrence and duration cannot be known in advance.
seoTitle: Belt Railway Chicago PTC maintenance request open for comment
seoDescription: FRA is reviewing Belt Railway of Chicago's request for four PTC network-maintenance windows, with comments due Sept. 1 and no approval yet.

headline: NIH Offers Cancer Methylation Classifier for Licensing
dek: The prototype platform uses 16,567 CNS reference profiles across 133 diagnostic classes and includes separate kidney-tumor work; commercialization and regulated deployment remain prospective.

sources.title: Government Owned Invention Available for License: DNA Methylation-Based Cancer Diagnostics for Accurate Tumor Classification

lead.creator: Linda Bartlett / National Cancer Institute
lead.rightsBasis: The National Cancer Institute released the official documentary photograph as a U.S. government public-domain work.
lead.attribution: Linda Bartlett / National Cancer Institute, public domain
lead.caption: Pathologists examine samples at microscopes in a National Cancer Institute photograph. NIH's licensing notice describes a molecular classifier intended to complement difficult tumor diagnosis.
lead.alt: Two pathologists in white laboratory coats looking into microscopes.

charts.caption: The CNS classifier uses 16,567 reference profiles organized into 22 tumor families and 133 diagnostic classes, including 21 newly developed classes.
charts.alt: Graphic shows 16,567 profiles, 22 tumor families, 133 classes and 21 newly developed classes.

charts.caption: In 1,204 NIH high-confidence validation cases, the notice says profiling confirmed 25.6%, refined 14.6%, increased precision for 54.7% and substantially reclassified 5.0%.
charts.alt: Graphic shows four percentages from the NIH clinical-impact analysis of 1,204 cases.

paragraphs: The National Institutes of Health is offering a DNA methylation-based cancer-classification platform for licensing and co-development.

The Aug. 12 notice describes the technology as a prototype, not a newly approved diagnostic product. Potential partners would still need validation, assay standardization, laboratory integration and any applicable regulated pathway before commercial clinical use.

Its central-nervous-system classifier was built from 16,567 curated methylation profiles organized into 22 tumor families and 133 clinically relevant classes. NIH says 21 of those classes are newly developed and not represented in other existing tools.

The classifier was evaluated across independent cohorts totaling 5,875 samples. In a separate clinical-impact analysis of 1,204 NIH high-confidence matches with earlier diagnoses available, methylation profiling affected the final diagnostic description in 74.4% of cases.
That 74.4% comprises refined subtyping in 14.6%, a new diagnosis with increased precision in 54.7% and substantial reclassification in 5.0%. The remaining 25.6% confirmed the initial diagnosis.

The platform also includes kidney-tumor work developed from more than 2,000 renal neoplasms. A classifier trained on 1,284 samples was externally tested on 287 and showed greater than 90% concordance for high-score classifications, according to the notice.

NIH has deployed a public-facing CNS workflow called MethylScape Analysis. Public software availability does not make every output a diagnosis or replace review by qualified pathology and clinical teams.

The agency seeks licensees and research collaborators for diagnostic tests or software-enabled classification. Commercial availability, performance in prospective practice, reimbursement and regulatory status remain unresolved.
facts: The CNS reference set contains 16,567 methylation profiles.
It spans 22 families and 133 diagnostic classes, including 21 newly developed classes.
Independent validation cohorts totaled 5,875 samples.
NIH labels the technology's development stage as prototype.
uncertainty: The licensing notice does not establish regulatory approval or commercial availability.
Retrospective and cohort performance may not predict results for every patient, laboratory or prospective workflow.
seoTitle: NIH offers DNA methylation cancer classifier for licensing
seoDescription: NIH's prototype cancer classifier uses 16,567 CNS methylation profiles and 133 classes; licensing, external validation and regulated deployment remain ahead.

headline: U.S. Mint Sets Trump Dollar Roll and Bag Prices
dek: A 25-coin roll will cost $61 and a 100-coin bag $154.50 starting Aug. 14; the one-ounce gold proof coin remains unpriced and precious-metal pricing can change weekly.

sources.title: Establish Prices for 2026 United States Mint Numismatic Products

lead.creator: Beyond My Ken
lead.rightsBasis: The photographer licensed the documentary U.S. Mint exterior photograph CC BY-SA 4.0 on Wikimedia Commons.
lead.caption: The United States Mint facility in Philadelphia. The Mint's Aug. 12 notice establishes prices for two 2026 dollar-coin roll and bag products.
lead.alt: Modern United States Mint building in Philadelphia viewed from the street.

charts.caption: Starting Aug. 14, the Mint lists $61 for a 25-coin roll and $154.50 for a 100-coin bag of the 2026 semiquincentennial Trump dollar.
charts.alt: Graphic compares 61-dollar roll and 154-dollar-and-50-cent bag prices.

charts.caption: The one-ounce 24-karat gold proof coin was listed as TBD; Mint precious-metal product prices can be evaluated weekly against the LBMA gold average.
charts.alt: Graphic shows gold proof coin price as to be determined and notes weekly precious-metal price review.

paragraphs: The United States Mint has set retail prices for two 2026 semiquincentennial dollar-coin products bearing President Donald J. Trump's name.
Starting Aug. 14, a 25-coin roll will cost $61 and a 100-coin bag will cost $154.50, according to the Mint's Federal Register notice.

Those totals work out to $2.44 per coin in the roll and $1.545 per coin in the bag before any shipping or order terms. The products are numismatic offerings, so their retail prices are above the coins' $1 face value.

The same notice lists the 2026 Semiquincentennial President Donald J. Trump 24-karat one-ounce gold proof coin price as to be determined. It does not announce a fixed retail price for that gold product.
Mint pricing for numismatic gold, palladium and platinum products can change weekly based on the London Bullion Market Association gold-price weekly average and the agency's pricing grid.

The notice establishes retail prices; it does not state product mintage, household ordering limits, release-hour availability or future resale value. Those details require separate Mint product records.
A lower per-coin price in the 100-coin bag does not by itself make either option an investment. Collector demand, condition, supply and later market prices are uncertain.
Buyers should use the Mint's current product page when sales open because availability and precious-metal pricing can change. This report is product-pricing news, not individualized financial advice.
facts: The 25-coin roll price is $61.
The 100-coin bag price is $154.50.
The prices take effect Aug. 14, 2026.
The one-ounce gold proof coin price remains to be determined in the notice.
uncertainty: The notice does not establish mintage, order limits, availability or resale value.
Precious-metal product prices can change under the Mint's weekly pricing method.
seoTitle: U.S. Mint sets 2026 Trump dollar roll and bag prices
seoDescription: The U.S. Mint set a $61 price for a 25-coin roll and $154.50 for a 100-coin bag, effective Aug. 14, while the gold proof price remains TBD.
